steps: Pour the footing
Reinforced concrete base below the frost line: 12" min thick, 6" beyond the footing on each side, 8 pieces of #4 rod at right angles, 4000 PSI min. Size it to dimensions D and E plus 12" each.
Foundation block + floor slab

Lay 8 x 12 x 16 block to 4" below finished floor, stepped in for the veneer (plus a 4" insulation barrier on outside builds). Cast a 4" slab level with the finished floor with 4 pieces of #4 rerod, kept off the outer veneer wall on outside construction.
Hearth layout + piers

Combustible side wall 19" min from the opening; raised hearth non-combustible, 16" in front and 8" each side, 10"–14" high, or a non-raised hearth 16" deep across the full face. The burning chamber sits on 4" block piers.
Masonry walls

Inner heat chamber of 4" lightweight or solid block, veneer 4" min with metal ties every course; hold dimension C. Where masonry runs outside the frame wall or into a garage, put 4" unfaced fiberglass between the walls down to grade (never polystyrene).
Set the chamber + outside air

Level the chamber on the piers with the front legs and clamp the furnished elbow and flex pipe to the air inlet. Run to a screened exterior termination above the snow line: 6" at or before 10 feet, 25' max, joints screwed or riveted and sealed with furnace cement.

Position the burning chamber on the block piers; the front legs adjust for leveling. Attach the furnished 90 degree elbow and flex pipe to the air inlet with the clamp.

  • Ducting more than 10 feet: increase to 6 inch at or before 10 feet.
  • No more than a 25' run; source the air from the closest point to the exterior.
  • Terminate to the building exterior, screened, above the snow line. Never in an attic, garage or unventilated crawl space. A screened vent is included.
  • Permanently secure every joint with sheet metal screws or pop rivets and seal with furnace cement.
  • Running through the building interior: adapt the aluminum pipe to class 1 insulated plastic duct after it exits the heat chamber, or condensation will occur.
Heat chamber + flue pipe

Build the inner walls so the upper slab base lands 72"–80" above the finished floor, the slab's finished top stays 12" min below ceiling headers or any other combustible, and the top block row is 16" min below the finished ceiling. Check the air control rod moves freely, then set the flue connection pipe into the flue outlet and attach it with metal screws (offsets 30 degrees max).
Cast the upper slab
4" min, 3000 psi, at least 7 reinforcement rods, on a dealer pour plate or a temporary plywood form, with 12" min to any wood framing. Remove every form and temporary support once it cures.

Thickness / mix4" min · 3000 psi
Reinforcement7 rods min (placement diagrams, p. 12)
To wood framing12" min, insulated with 6" unfaced fiberglass after the chimney is complete

The pour plate overlaps the side and back heat chamber walls by 2" and carries the slab until it cures; on an outside installation ring it with 4" block so the slab can't touch the outer veneer. Alternative: a plywood form on temporary posts, cut in half and cleated for removal. Keep concrete out of the insulation space. Any plywood or combustible left in the heat chamber will burn.

Seismic zones: #4 reinforcement per chapter 10 of the IRC, end bent and tied to the vertical fireplace rods; at least four #4 rods end bent, tied to the slab rods and run vertically. Chimney to NFPA 211.
Chimney adapter + chimney

Set the adapter in the flue pipe, suspended for expansion, and fill beneath it with masonry cement; then build the clay tile (8x12 O.D. min) or class A 2100 degree metal (8" ID) chimney. Keep 2" to combustibles and terminate 3' above a flat roof or 2' above anything within 10'.

Place the chimney adapter into the flue connection pipe with its base suspended above the pipe to allow expansion. Ring it with brick or block and fill the void down to the slab with masonry cement. Failure to use the adapter may cause a creosote leak and voids the warranties.

Clay tile (Diagram FC1)

Set the first flue tile in the clay tile adapter and build block or brick around it. 8x12 O.D. tile min; 12 x 12 O.D. recommended when using less than 12 foot of clay tile liner. 4" min masonry encasement, preferably insulated between liner and encasement. Build to chapter 10 of the IRC and NFPA 211.

Metal chimney (Diagram FC2)

Class A 2100 degree, 8" inner diameter, per the chimney maker. Use the dealer's adapter, attach a chimney starter plate and skip the clay tile step.

Keep 2" to combustibles. Terminate 3' above a flat roof, or 2' above any point within 10' of the closest peak. Never use the chimney or fireplace as structural support for framing.
Veneer, mantel + louvers

Fit 1/2" x 4" unfaced fiberglass expansion joints, 3/8" expansion room and a lintel iron so nothing touches the burning chamber. Set the upper louver flush with the slab bottom, fins down, and seal the face wall to the upper slab with cement.

• Expansion joints: unfaced fiberglass 1/2 inch thick, 4 inches wide, between the burning chamber side walls and the masonry, and between the back and bottom of the lintel and the top of the chamber.
  • At least 3/8 inches expansion room between masonry face and burning chamber; lintel iron across the face opening. No metal or masonry may contact the chamber.
  • Combustible mantel: 24 inches min from top of opening to bottom of mantel; top no closer than 8 inches to the bottom of the heat outlet louver; 14 inches max depth. Masonry must carry the mantel load.
  • Upper louver: top flush with the bottom of the upper slab, fins down; a pocket reduces circulation. A masonry inlet/outlet instead of the louver needs 210 sq. inches open area.
  • Face wall to ceiling height; fill the face wall / upper slab void with cement. A forced-air cold air return in the ceiling above the outlet louver is recommended; never connect the fireplace directly to the forced air system.
Doors, refractory + cure

Clean the face wall (no caustic solvents), install the doors with the thermotape seal, then the Skamol panels and steel baffle. No fires for at least 3 weeks after completion; leave the instructions and warranty card with the owner.

Doors: only a Wilkening door completes the listed unit. Remove the paper backing from the heat resistant gasket and apply it to the unit face on the outside edge of the predrilled holes around the opening, then attach the frame with the 8 screws from the door carton, using the anti-seize provided.

Refractory order (diagram on p. 10)

  1. Two upper side panes above the side air tube (#6)
  2. Two bottom pieces (#1 and #2)
  3. Two piece back panel (#3), joined at the top center edge with the stainless "U" clip
  4. Four side pieces (#4), each front one before its back one
  5. Panel #5 over the top edge of the air tubes, resting on the back panel
  6. Two piece refractory top baffle plate on the dual stainless air tubes

The steel baffle with holes sits on the metal tabs in the upper throat, above the secondary combustion air tubes. Never run the unit without every baffle and liner piece in place.

Don't let the owner fire it for at least 3 weeks from completion. Premature use deteriorates the masonry cement and causes cracking.

panels.title: Smoke spills out when the doors open
items: Excessive or wet fuel → over capacity, or low draft from a cool firebox
Chimney blocked (leaves, nest) or heavy creosote → poor draw
Chimney too short (must clear anything within 10' by 2') or offsets → add height
Doors opened fast → vortex; open both together, slowly
Sudden smoking after normal operation → plugged cap or fallen creosote blocking the upper baffle holes

panels.title: Smoky glass / smoldering fire
items: Wet wood, fire too small, or door closed too soon after lighting → firebox too cool
Air supply closed with a fire burning → heavy smoke on the glass
Stacked or overloaded firebox → smoldering, smoky fire
Large, un-split or tightly stacked wood → slower fire, more smoke on glass

panels.title: Poor draft at start-up
items: Tight home, stack effect → negative pressure; air drops down the chimney when the doors open
Close windows above, open one on the fireplace level (windward side)
Light crumpled newspaper with doors closed and air open to start the draw
Exterior chimney below 0° Fahrenheit, or basement unit with outside chimney → poor draft, flow reversal on start up

panels.title: Overheating
items: Inlet or outlet circulation grills blocked → structure overheats
Lower louver blocked → poor circulation, overheated masonry
Heat outlet louver misplaced → excessive temperatures; a pocket at the louver → reduced circulation
Baffles or inner liner missing → chimney connector overheats
Cardboard, paper or rapidly combustible loads → steel structure overheats

light.title: Starting a fire
light.html:
The combustion air lever is at the lower left of the door frame. Open it before you light.

  1. Lift the lever. A spring opens the outside air supply.
  2. Lay 2 large split logs on the base of the fireplace, cut ends pointing to each side.
  3. On top, lay a row of smaller split wood with the cut ends pointing toward the back.
  4. Add crumpled newspaper or a fire starter, then fine split kindling and a few small split pieces over and around it.
  5. Light the starter and close the door. The fire burns from the top down.
  6. When the large logs are burned down, add more wood on top.

Build the fire right on the base. Don't use a grate or andirons. Crisscrossed wood lets air in under the fire.

Air coming down the chimney when you open the doors? That means negative pressure in the house. Close windows on the floors above, open one on the fireplace level, then light a few crumpled sheets of newspaper with the doors closed and the air open to get the chimney drawing.
Note: the owner's manual (p. 2) gives this top-down method for starting a fire, lit with the door closed. The installation manual (p. 19) puts 8-10 sheets of crumpled newspaper in the center with two small split logs on each side and kindling on top, and leaves the door ajar for 8-10 minutes, then adds kindling and closes the doors.

firstfire.title: Your first fires
firstfire.html:
A new masonry fireplace needs a gentle start.

  • Let the masonry cure. Your installer is told not to let you use the fireplace for at least 3 weeks after the work is finished. Using it sooner can break down the masonry cement and cause cracking.
  • Keep the first fires small and short: less than one hour each, with no fast-burning material such as building scrap or siding. Make the very first fire especially short. It drives most of the moisture out of the refractory liner (the panels lining the firebox) and cures the gasket cement.
  • Expect an odor and some smoke. The high-heat paint is curing and oils on the outer metal are burning off. Keep the room well ventilated. People who are allergic to smoke or asthmatic shouldn't be there during this curing.
  • Expect dirty glass. Creosote stains may cover the whole glass, because these small fires aren't hot enough for it to "self-clean."
Note: the owner's manual says to keep the first two to three fires small (p. 2); the installation manual says the first two (p. 19).

air.title: The combustion air control
air.html:
The GranView is a single burn rate fireplace. Its outside air supply, the air that feeds the fire, is either open or closed. There's no setting in between.

While a fire is burning

  • Lift the lever at the lower left of the door frame. A spring opens the supply.
  • Keep it open the whole time. Closing it starves the fire, lets gases build up in the firebox and coats the glass with heavy smoke.

When you're not using the fireplace

Push the handle in and lock it in the notch cut into the lever. That stops air flowing through, which would otherwise cool the steel and carry cold into the room.

For the most heat

Burn smaller, split wood. The fire is at its best when the flames burn clean and clear.

Never plug the outside air supply or run a fire with it closed. Gases can build up inside the fireplace and may cause an explosion or heavy creosote. In a chimney fire, push the lever in to the locked position (see Safety).

refuel.title: Adding wood without smoke
refuel.html:
1. Crack the doors open for 15 seconds to clear the smoke. If you open both doors, crack them at the same time, slowly, then open them fully.
  2. Add wood onto a hot coal bed. Don't stack or overload the firebox. That makes a smoldering, smoky fire.

A hot firebox minimizes smoke on the glass and creosote in the chimney. Keep the wood behind the log retainer so burning pieces can't spill out when you open the door.

Smoke coming into the room?

  • Too much wood, or wet wood, can push smoke out when the door opens.
  • Opening both doors together, slowly, cuts the swirl of incoming air that pulls smoke out.
  • A chimney blocked by leaves, a nest or creosote draws poorly, and so does one that's too short. With offsets it may need extra height. Ask your dealer.
  • Smoking suddenly after working fine? Check that the chimney cap isn't plugged and that fallen creosote isn't blocking the holes in the top baffle.
Note: the owner's manual (p. 3) says that with a large fire you may open just the right-hand door to refuel, to cut the radiant heat. The installation manual (p. 18) says to crack both doors open at the same time to refuel, and warns the doors must be run with both fully open or fully closed.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Clean the glass only when the fireplace has cooled to room temperature.

  • Use an ammonia-based cleaner, a fireplace glass cleaner, or Speedy White (from your dealer or Wilkening).
  • Keep cleaner off the painted and plated surfaces, which it can discolor. Cleaner mixed with creosote also hardens the gaskets.
  • Wipe off the smoke and cleaner residue with a soft cotton cloth or paper towel.
  • Never scrape with razor blades or abrasive pads. That damages the glass and may make it fail.

Some smoke on the glass is normal

After a series of fires the outer edges cloud over, usually in a band less than 2" wide, and won't burn clean. If the glass smokes over in a low fire or at the end of a fire, build a large fire and let the heat burn it off. Heavy smoke means the fire runs too cool: wet wood, too small a fire, or closing the door too soon after lighting.

If the glass breaks, replace it with a similar 1400 degree ceramic glass from your dealer or Wilkening. Regular or tempered glass can't take the heat. Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the fireplace.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn only solid wood or processed solid fuel fire logs. Dry, split wood gives the most heat and the least creosote.

  • Dry: well-seasoned, air-dried wood with less than 20% moisture. Wood that sizzles in the fire is too wet and makes heavy creosote. Moisture meters are available through your dealer.
  • Split: smaller split pieces give the greatest heat. Large, un-split or tightly stacked wood burns slower and smokes up the glass.
  • Fire logs: only logs evaluated and listed for use in a fireplace. Read the warnings on the package first.

Never burn

  • Coal or charcoal
  • Treated wood, or wood that has been in saltwater
  • Loads of cardboard, paper or other fast-burning material, which overheat the steel
  • Gas logs, gas starters or flame colorants
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, lighter fluid or any other liquid to start or "freshen" a fire. Keep those liquids well away from the fireplace.

chimney.title: Chimney care & creosote
chimney.html:
Creosote is a black deposit that forms when smoke condenses in the cool flue of a slow-burning fire. Wet wood makes more of it. If it ignites it burns extremely hot and can start a chimney fire.

How often to check

  • Wilkening recommends inspecting the chimney monthly and cleaning it if needed, and at a minimum twice during the heating season.
  • Don't let more than 1/8 inch build up between cleanings.
  • Have a certified chimney sweep or your dealer inspect the whole system every year before the first fire, even if you clean the chimney yourself.

Cleaning

Professional cleaning is recommended. If you do it yourself:

  1. Remove the steel and refractory baffles at the top of the firebox (the throat) and the angled refractory panel above the fire, so falling creosote drops to the base.
  2. Remove the chimney cap and use a stiff plastic/poly brush. Metal brushes scratch and damage the stainless steel chimney.
  3. Clean the creosote out of the firebox before your next fire.
  4. Put the baffles and the angled refractory panel back. Never run the fireplace without all the baffles and inner liner in place: the chimney connector and fireplace parts may overheat.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
1. Wait until the fire is out and the ashes are cold.
  2. Empty the ashes into a metal container with a lid. Never use a cardboard box. Your dealer has a special ash bucket that makes this easier.
  3. Close the lid tight and set the container on a noncombustible surface or the ground, well away from anything that can burn.
  4. Don't store ashes in your home.

If you bury the ashes or spread them outdoors, keep them in the closed container until all the cinders have thoroughly cooled.

Hot coals in the ash can stay dangerous for several days after you remove them.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. Push the combustion air control in to the locked position.
  2. Make sure the doors are fully closed.
  3. Call the fire department, alert your family and get everyone out.

Don't use the fireplace again until a certified sweep or another qualified chimney and fireplace professional has inspected the whole system.

Everyday safety

  • Keep furniture and anything else that can burn at least 3 feet from the front.
  • Never leave children unattended with a fire burning.
  • Never block the circulation grills, the inlet at the base or the heat outlet above.
  • Keep the fire behind the log retainer and never against the glass. Don't slam the doors.
  • Don't over-fire it: that damages the fireplace and can cause a structure fire. Never run it with broken or missing firebrick panels.
  • Keep a multi-purpose fire extinguisher nearby. A smoke detector and a carbon monoxide detector in the room are recommended.
  • Let it cool, and shut off any electrical supply, before you service it.

warranty.title: GranView 10 year warranty
warranty.html:
Wilkening's limited warranty covers the original retail purchaser, counted from the date of purchase.

Control rods and knobs, gasket seals, electrical components, refractory liner1 year
Door frame and all metal parts and components10 years

For a defective metal part

  • First year: Wilkening repairs or replaces it at no cost.
  • 2nd through 5th year: a replacement part at no cost.
  • 6th through 10th year: a replacement part at 50% of the then current retail price.

Labor, postage and freight aren't covered, and neither are parts made by others, such as painted or electroplated surfaces.

What can void it

  • Alterations, improper installation, abuse, neglect or over firing
  • No chimney cap installed
  • Installing it outside the continental United States or Canada, or moving it from where it was first installed
Register within 60 days. The warranty only takes effect if your completed owner's registration card reaches Wilkening within 60 days of purchase. It doesn't transfer to a later owner.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:
Factory-built8" inner diameter, listed to UL-103HT; one brand only
Masonry8 x 12 clay lined min (8x12 O.D. clay flue tile)
Less than 12 foot of clay tile12 x 12 O.D. flue recommended
Metal (class A 2100 degree)8" inner diameter, starter plate on the adapter
Total height15' min to 36' max, base of unit to cap
Termination2' above any roof or wall within 10'; 3' above a chase top or flat roof
Offset30 degree max; no more than two sets of 30 degree elbows
To combustibles2" min, left empty
Typical framing, 8" 2100 degree HT14-1/2" x 14-1/2"

Factory-built: anchor plate fixed with 4 self tapping metal screws and sealed to the flue adaptor with 600 degree RTV silicone; firestop and/or radiation shield at each combustible penetration (flashing or chase top at the roof); sealed storm collar; roof support; roof brace if more than 6' is exposed above the roof. The factory offset pipe counts as 1 set of offsets; keep at least one pipe section between elbows. Masonry chimneys: 4" min masonry encasement. A chimney cap is required to validate the warranty. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance. Multiple flues in one chase: terminations recommended at least 16" apart horizontally and 12" vertically.

specAir.title: Outside combustion air
specAir.html:
Outside air feeds every combustion air port, a sealed supply. The hook-up is on the lower left of the fireplace as you face it.

Supply pipe4" diameter min
More than ten feet6" pipe, reduced to 4" at the unit connection
Maximum25' of duct; no more than three 90 degree bends
5' or lessstandard air kit with screened exterior vent termination
  • Terminate outside, screened, above the snow line. Never in an attic, garage or unventilated crawl space.
  • Only noncombustible supply lines inside the masonry chamber; insulated class 1 duct outside it, against cold transfer and condensation.
  • The inlet must not rise vertically inside the heat chamber (reverse exhaust flow when the doors open). Ducting from above: exit the back or side wall via the 90 degree elbow and the 5' of flexible aluminum provided.
  • Install the duct with an "S" trap to minimize air flow when the unit isn't operating.

specClear.title: Clearances
specClear.html:
Combustible mantel24" min above the door opening
Top of combustible mantel8" min below the upper heat outlet
Combustible mantel depth14" max
Non-combustible mantelany height
Combustible side wall to opening19" min
Combustibles above the upper slab12" min
Chimney to framing, supports, insulation2" min
Combustibles in front, incl. furniture3 feet

Additional clearance is permitted. The outside air kit, fire stop spacer and roof flashings may sit directly on or next to normal construction materials. Don't pack or fill the required air spaces; no material of any kind inside the masonry heat chamber, so insulate only on its outside.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension
specHearth.html:
Raised hearth16" in front, 8" each side of the opening; all non-combustible
Raised hearth height10" min to 14" max (see note)
Floor to finished ceiling88" min for a raised hearth
Floor level hearth16" min (20" recommended), plus 8" side protection
Over a combustible floor1/2" thick Micore 300 under the hearth material

The manual's step 3 (p. 11) also requires a non-raised hearth to extend 16" in front and completely across the face of the fireplace (Diagram 3S). The bottom of the burning chamber must sit at least 8" above the hearth extension so the lower louver fits below the firebox; don't let hearth material block that room air inlet. For a raised hearth, the metal plate provided rests the hearth stone on a 4 x 8 x 16 block.

Note: p. 11 says a raised hearth should be no less than 10" and no more than 14" high; the raised hearth installation drawing (Diagram 2, p. 6) labels the hearth height 10 to 12".

specMasonry.title: Masonry structure
specMasonry.html:
Masonry walls2-4" thick walls with 4" of insulation between, or 1-4" wall with 6" of insulation to combustibles
Inner heat chamber4" lightweight or 4" solid block; don't alter dimensions B or G (width and depth)
Outer veneerbrick, stone or block, 4" min
Base of upper slab72" min, 80" max from finished floor
Top row of block16" min to finished ceiling
Min finished frame opening60" wide, 88" tall, 40" deep from finished face
Framing1-1/2 x 3-1/2" min, covered with sheeting

Carry it on a masonry foundation from the frost footing through any combustible floor, never on combustible framing or an interior slab on grade. Exterior chases: insulate sides, back and ceiling to the R value of the other exterior walls. Local codes may require a one hour fire rating. The lettered dimensions are drawings on p. 6 (Diagrams 1–3) and p. 15 (corner and stacked units); work from those.

Note: p. 4 calls for 4" of insulation between two 4" masonry walls, p. 11 requires a 4" unfaced fiberglass barrier between them wherever the masonry chamber extends outside the frame wall or into a garage, and p. 15 labels the gaps as 4" insulated spaces, but the same p. 15 drawing says its dimensions are for two 4" walls with 2" of insulation.

specFooting.title: Footing & slabs
specFooting.html:
Footing12" min thick, at least 6" beyond each side, below the frost line
Footing sizedimensions D and E plus 12" each
Footing mix / rebar4000 PSI min; 8 pieces of #4 rod at right angles
Foundation block8 x 12 x 16, up to 4" below finished floor
Floor level slab4" thick, level with finished floor; 4 pieces of #4 rerod cross lapped and tied
Upper slab4" min thick, 3000 psi, 7 reinforcement rods min

On outside construction, keep the slabs off the outer veneer wall or severe cold transfer will occur. Remove all forms and temporary supports after the upper slab cures. Seismic zones: reinforcement per chapter 10 of the IRC (see "Cast the upper slab" in the install sequence).

specBlower.title: Optional blower
specBlower.html:
An onboard blower boosts the heat circulation system when the lower louver is used for the air inlet.

Blowertwo speed, twin squirrel cage fan
Locationbase of the fireplace, center, 4" behind the lower grill
Controllow/off/high switch; high side may go to a wall-mounted rheostat, white as neutral
  • Wire nut all connections; keep every wire off the unit's steel surfaces or the insulation can melt.
  • Ground the fireplace through the metal electrical box behind the lower louver.
  • Follow the instructions and electrical information in the fan kit.

The wiring (110 VAC to a terminal block) is shown as a diagram on p. 9; work from the drawing.

conflicts.issue: Fire-starting method differs. Owner's manual: 2 large split logs on the base, a row of smaller split wood, then paper/starter and kindling on top; light and close the door (top-down burn). Installation manual: 8-10 sheets of crumpled newspaper in the center, two small split logs each side, kindling on top; leave the door ajar 8-10 minutes, then add kindling and close. Owner's manual p. 3 also lists closing the door too soon after lighting as a cause of smoky glass.
Break-in fires: owner's manual says the first two to three fires should be small and short (less than one hour); installation manual says the first two.

Owner's manual suggests opening only the right-hand door to refuel a large fire; installation manual says to crack both doors at the same time to refuel and warns doors must be operated with both fully open or fully closed.

Insulation between the two masonry walls: 4" on p. 4 (two 4" walls); p. 11 requires a 4" unfaced fiberglass barrier wherever the masonry chamber extends outside the frame wall or into a garage (and p. 15 says gaps are 4" insulated spaces), but the p. 15 drawing note says its dimensions are for two 4" walls with 2" of insulation.
Raised hearth height: 10" to 14" in step 3 (p. 11); Diagram 2, the raised hearth installation drawing (p. 6), labels it 10 to 12".

catalog_mismatches.manual: Outside air is the standard, required supply: it feeds every combustion air port, a standard air kit comes with the fireplace, and the manual says never to plug it or operate with it closed (p. 8, p. 20).
catalog_mismatches.website_note: No Maker's website note added: website.json has no outside-air row (only the page description and door options), so there is no website wording to quote.

review.notes: Wood-burning masonry fireplace: no ignition system and no code table, so codes is empty. Catalog firebox volume (4.2 cu ft), recommended log length (24 in), emissions (2.72 g/kg), weight (525 lb), blower CFM and EPA status are not stated in either manual, so they are left out and could not be checked. Catalog says UL 127 / UL 1482; the manual names only UL 127-2011 (Intertek), doc 1 p. 4. Lettered masonry dimensions (Diagrams 1-3 on doc 1 p. 6; corner/stacked layout on p. 15), the reinforcement-rod placement drawings (p. 12) and adapter drawings FC1/FC2 (p. 13) are figures: no lettered values transcribed; only B/G (inner chamber width/depth) and D/E (+12 in for footing) are referenced by name as the text does. Diagram 1 on p. 6 carries a '10 to 12' label that may be the raised hearth height, while step 3 (p. 11) says 10-14 in; worth a visual check.
